sketches.title: Habit Headstone
sketches.premise: We are burying a habit with one dramatic gravestone inscription. Both players get the same ordinary habit and write a tiny epitaph that makes its death sound like a legendary event; the sharpest inscription wins the crowd. Step up to the monument—your first bad routine is already in the ground!
sketches.criterion: The inscription must clearly mourn the dealt habit while presenting its ending as a specific, grand, checkable change.
sketches.move_shape: Write one inscription of up to 160 characters, naming the habit and its transformed replacement without stating the real-life reason it ended; example for “checking your phone”: “Here lies checking my phone—at last replaced by checking the sky.”
sketches.first_card: Habit: leaving clothes on the floor. Hidden truth: the host knows why this habit ended.

sketches.title: Last Words Laundry
sketches.premise: A habit is dead, and its final words must be delivered from the stone. Both players receive the same habit plus two everyday nouns and write one farewell that links them; the judge rewards the cleanest emotional hit. Cue the trumpet—this routine gets one last speech!
sketches.criterion: The farewell must keep the habit recognizable and connect both given nouns in a sincere or comic final statement.
sketches.move_shape: Write one sentence using the habit and both nouns, without revealing which noun is the hidden cause of death; example with “snacking,” “backpack,” and “moon”: “Snacking leaves its backpack by the moon and promises not to return.”
sketches.first_card: Habit: saying “just five more minutes.” Nouns: alarm, blanket. Hidden truth: one noun is the real witness.

sketches.title: Epitaph Switcheroo
sketches.premise: Every habit gets a stone, but the inscription must make its worst feature sound like a heroic legacy. Both players use the same habit and two nouns, then the judge decides who pulled off the bolder transformation without losing the habit’s identity. Behold: the puny routine enters, and a legend leaves!
sketches.criterion: The inscription must preserve the habit’s everyday behavior while turning it into a legacy that includes both nouns.
sketches.move_shape: Write one headline-like epitaph using the habit and both nouns, with no claim about why it stopped; example for “procrastinating,” “calendar,” and “seed”: “Procrastinating: planted a calendar, harvested tomorrow.”
sketches.first_card: Habit: interrupting people. Nouns: door, drum. Hidden truth: the door was present at the final incident.

sketches.title: Stone-Cold Replacement
sketches.premise: A habit has been carved into history, and its gravestone must announce what replaced it. Both players get the same habit and two nouns and write a compact inscription that makes the replacement sound inevitable; the judge crowns the move that travels furthest while staying clear. The old routine is rubble—build something astonishing on top of it!
sketches.criterion: The inscription must state or unmistakably imply a replacement for the habit and use both nouns as parts of that replacement.
sketches.move_shape: Write one epitaph of up to 160 characters, using the habit and both nouns, without saying which noun supplied the replacement idea; example for “staying up late,” “candle,” and “window”: “Here lies staying up late; the candle now sleeps by the window.”
sketches.first_card: Habit: forgetting homework. Nouns: bridge, pencil. Hidden truth: the pencil marks the real replacement.

sketches.title: Mourning Mistake
sketches.premise: The monument is ready, but the inscription must praise the habit for the one useful thing it accidentally did before it vanished. Both players receive the same habit and two nouns, then write a memorial that makes the accident feel historic; the judge applauds the most convincing tribute. Roll the stone into place—this blunder gets a parade!
sketches.criterion: The memorial must keep the habit identifiable and give it one accidental benefit involving both nouns without revealing the hidden real-world event.
sketches.move_shape: Write one sentence that memorializes the habit and credits it with an accidental result involving both nouns; example for “losing pencils,” “map,” and “garden”: “Losing pencils left a map of the garden, and no one dared erase it.”
sketches.first_card: Habit: talking to yourself. Nouns: mirror, captain. Hidden truth: the captain is the real person involved.

sketches.title: Graveyard Greatest Hit
sketches.premise: A dead habit gets one final headline for the history books. Both players receive the same habit and two nouns and write a punchy newspaper-style inscription about its last great achievement; the judge awards the headline that sounds biggest without giving away the hidden truth. Front page, black border, full drama—print your move!
sketches.criterion: The headline must identify the habit, use both nouns, and describe a plausible final achievement without disclosing the card’s checkable hidden truth.
sketches.move_shape: Write a headline or one-line epitaph using the habit and both nouns, avoiding any explicit cause of death; example for “avoiding chores,” “rocket,” and “broom”: “AVOIDING CHORES LAUNCHES A ROCKET, LEAVING THE BROOM TO CLAIM THE HOUSE.”
sketches.first_card: Habit: eating breakfast too fast. Nouns: whistle, bridge. Hidden truth: the whistle was sounded at the real final attempt.
